data.title: Do Security Cameras Make Us Feel Safer or Give Us Unnecessary Frights? — WSJ
data.description:
By Julie Jargon

Amanda Presswood was in her upstairs bedroom last month when she checked her Ring doorbell camera to see if it was raining. It was dry out. She watched as two cars drove down the quiet street beyond her porch.

Then she heard voices.

The first was a male voice, followed by women's voices. The speech was garbled, but to Presswood it sounded like the male voice asked, "Can I talk to you?" There was nobody on camera.

Presswood lives with her adult son in a 93-year-old house in Galesburg, Ill., a small town not far from the Iowa border. The school-bus attendant had been spooked by unsettling anomalies before — footsteps when no one's around, the TV suddenly powering on — but she figured there was a reasonable explanation for this incident.

"I've watched those paranormal shows and a lot of the stories can be debunked, so I tried to debunk it," she says.

Her son wasn't home. Presswood knew her neighbors weren't home either, and that no one was at the church across the street. She panned around with the camera and didn't see anyone. She went outside but there was no sign of anyone.

So far, her ghostly story remains a mystery.

Home-security cameras are meant to reduce the anxiety we feel from the unknown: Who's at the door? How is the baby sleeping? What's happening at home when we're on vacation? And these cameras do provide solace, occasionally serving to prevent problematic behavior and even criminal acts.

There are cases, however, when the video feed only fuels our worries. And in rare instances, what we see can be inexplicable — or downright terrifying.

Christine Peck, owner of the Sock Monkey Kids Shop in Cape May County, N.J., received a motion alert from the store's Ring camera one day in August 2024. The shop was closed. She figured an employee had left something and had gone in to retrieve it, but no one was inside.

Instead, she saw a black shadowy mist drifting around the room filled with toys.

Mysterious things have happened at the shop before. Several times plush toys have fallen off shelves with seemingly no intervention. The wispy apparition was the last straw. She turned off the camera alerts.

"I don't look anymore," she says. "I don't want to know."

Peck's area actually made this year's list of spookiest cities in America: Cape May was ranked sixth by home-security company Vivint. The company creates its ranking based on reported ghost sightings and haunted locations, among other criteria.

Ken Weeks would concur. Two years ago, he was at his winter home in Sanford, Fla., when he got a door alert from the Samsung refrigerator in his house in Cape May. Sure enough, on his Ring camera, he could see the door open slowly on its own. He even heard the ding the fridge makes when someone waves their hand under the door sensor to open it. He got chills.

Weeks asked a neighbor to check the house. Nobody was there, and there was no sign of entry.

"Being a skeptic, my first reaction was that it was a technical glitch," says Weeks, who works for a software company. "But we haven't been able to come up with a rational explanation for how that happened."

The door hasn't spontaneously opened again — though some people have complained on Reddit about the same model opening randomly. Samsung didn't respond to requests for comment.

Not all unexplained occurrences are unwelcome.

Emily Pendergast, an actress in Los Angeles, had set up a SimpliSafe indoor camera with her husband in the spring of 2024 so they could keep tabs on their new rescue pit-bull-mix puppy, Winter.

One day, while out grocery shopping, they got a motion alert. Her husband pulled out his phone.

"He stopped dead in his tracks," Pendergast recalls.

For a moment, they saw what appeared to be Lang, the beloved rescue shepherd mix they had had for nearly 13 years. Only Lang died in 2023.

Pendergast held on to the video and watched it over and over again. Earlier this month, she decided to post it on Instagram because she felt it might bring comfort to others who have lost pets. The video garnered more than seven million views. Pendergast likes to think Lang is watching over Winter.

"I felt we were able to see something we weren't intended to see," Pendergast says.

Write to Julie Jargon at Julie.Jargon@wsj.com

data.title: Ambuja Neotia, IHCL to invest up to ₹3,000 crore in 9 hospitality projects in Bengal
data.description:
The Ambuja Neotia Group will invest around ₹3,000 crore over the next five to seven years on nine projects in West Bengal’s hospitality sector in partnership with the Indian Hotels Company Ltd (IHCL), officials said on Saturday.

The upcoming projects in the state are spread across Kolkata, Raichak, Digha, Siliguri, Lataguri, Kalimpong and Darjeeling, said Harshavardhan Neotia, Chairman, Ambuja Neotia Group.

Neotia, along with MD and CEO of IHCL, Puneet Chhatwal, on Saturday unveiled the AltAir House – IHCL SeleQtions – in Kolkata and Siliguri.

Ambuja Neotia and IHCL now operate 11 hospitality projects in the state, and the number would rise to 20 with the completion of the nine other facilities, Neotia said.

"West Bengal offers an extraordinary diversity of landscapes and cultural experiences, from its vibrant cities and riverfronts to its forests, tea gardens and the Himalayas. Our investment commitment of about ₹2,700-3,000 crore reflects our confidence in the region’s tourism potential," Neotia said.

The investment amount includes the two newly launched hotels and ₹100 crore expansion of Taj Chia Kutir Resort & Spa, Darjeeling, with 28 keys and 15,000 square feet of banqueting facilities, he said.

The upcoming projects under their collaboration include the Taj Ananta Kutir & Taj Uvanta Signature Residences, Kolkata, with an inventory of 248 keys and 354 apartments, the Taj Himya Kutir & Taj Himya Branded Villas in Darjeeling’s Ghoom with 57 keys and 10 villas, and the Taj Terai Kutir, Siliguri, with 140 keys.

"IHCL and Ambuja Neotia are committed to advancing tourism, creating new travel experiences, and expanding the presence of IHCL’s brands across the region," Chhatwal said.

Ambuja Neotia, and IHCL’s partnership consists of a portfolio of over 80 properties across India, including 55 resorts under Tree of Life, an experiential leisure brand, Chhatwal said.

Neotia said West Bengal has always been a focus area for the Kolkata-headquartered diversified corporate group, and that he had recently met Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari to present a company vision about investments in the state.

"We will invest around ₹15,000 crore in hospitality, healthcare and real estate over the next five to seven years. The ₹2,700-3,000 crore investment commitment is part of this vision," he said.

Chhatwal said the travel, tourism and hospitality sector is the highest multiplicator of jobs, creating a lot of indirect employment.

"So, we are not only developing infrastructure for the growth of tourism, but also creating a lot of employment and income stream for the state in various forms, whether it’s through services, income taxes or GST," he added.

data.title: The stock market's front-runners stumbled in October. Here's where the smart money is moving now.
data.description:
By Christine Idzelis

Investors are shifting money into stocks with defensive and high-quality characteristics

Investors were spooked by the tech selloff in October.

U.S. stocks saw a strong reversal in fortunes in October, as worries about dwindling free cash flows and rising borrowing costs threw a wrench into the artificial-intelligence trade.

Tech stocks were punished, with the S&P 500's information-technology sector XX:SP500.45 snapping back-to-back monthly gains to drop 6.8% for its worst month since March 2025, FactSet data showed. Investors - spooked by fears that companies may not deliver the payoff they had expected from AI despite continuing to pour money into building data centers - leaned into traditionally more defensive parts of the equities market. They're also eyeing high-quality stocks to help mitigate sudden tech blows.

Friday's clobbering of the Invesco S&P 500 Momentum ETF SPMO, which tracks stocks in the U.S. large-cap equities index that have a high momentum score and whose portfolio is heavily weighted toward tech, left the exchange-traded fund with a 10.1% loss in October. The iShares MSCI USA Momentum Factor ETF MTUM, which seeks to capture market trends by investing in U.S. stocks with strong recent performance, booked a similar drop of 10.5% in October, according to FactSet data.

"We're buying quality," said Jeff Buchbinder, chief equity strategist at LPL Financial, in a phone interview. "When you buy quality products, you are getting a little bit of a value tilt, and you're getting a little bit of underweight to the AI trade, particularly to the lower-quality segment of the AI trade."

Marta Norton, Empower's chief investment strategist, also pointed to stocks with quality characteristics as desirable in the current environment, citing their "lower levels of debt, consistent earnings streams and a measure of growth embedded in the revenue profile."

While tech's struggles in October dragged the S&P 500 SPX and Nasdaq Composite Index COMP into the red, high-quality stocks generally appeared to hold up amid the AI-related carnage.

Take the iShares MSCI USA Quality Factor ETF QUAL, which aims to invest in U.S. stocks with stable earnings and low debt. The fund ended October with a slight 0.1% gain, according to FactSet data. By contrast, the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell 5.3% in October, cementing its worst monthly performance since March 2025, according to Dow Jones Market Data.

As the AI trade's recent comeback violently reversed in October, investors have sought shelter in Treasury bonds while also taking cover in traditionally defensive stock-market sectors, like healthcare XX:SP500.35, utilities XX:SP500.55 and consumer staples XX:SP500.30.

The State Street Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR ETF XLP, the State Street Utilities Select Sector SPDR ETF XLU and the State Street Health Care Select Sector SPDR ETF XLV all saw enormous rallies in October.

The consumer staples ETF, whose top three holdings as of Thursday included Walmart (WMT), Costco Wholesale (COST) and Procter & Gamble Co. (PG), soared 10.9% in October. That huge gain left the State Street Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR ETF with its largest monthly gain ever since it began trading in 1998, according to Dow Jones Market Data.

While consumers still appear to be spending despite sticky inflation, purchases of discretionary items risk falling off if the stock market experiences a big drawdown that makes investors worried about a drop in their wealth, Russell Price, chief economist at Ameriprise Financial, told MarketWatch by phone. But consumer staples tend to fare relatively well when the economy slows, as people continue to shop for items like soap, toothpaste and shampoo.

Consumer staples tend to be "a safer place to be within the equity market," said Empower's Norton, "as there's just not a whole lot of earnings volatility there." But she cautioned that, at this point, the consumer-staples sector appears "overvalued" following its recent surge.

The S&P 500's consumer-staples sector has gained almost 16% this year after its October spike, according to FactSet data.

Still, the index's tech sector has seen an even bigger gain so far in 2026 - around 19% - despite fears over the AI trade as chip stocks sold off in October.

The PHLX Semiconductor Index SOX plunged more than 15% in October, with Intel's shares (INTC) plummeting 28.6% on Friday alone after the company's quarterly earnings report disappointed investors.

Big Tech stocks also fell Friday, as investors digested Amazon.com's (AMZN) quarterly earning results. The Roundhill Magnificent Seven ETF MAGS - whose holdings include seven Big Tech stocks including Amazon, Nvidia (NVDA), Google parent Alphabet (GOOG) (GOOGL), Microsoft (MSFT), Facebook parent Meta Platforms (META) and Tesla (TSLA) - dropped 4.5% in October, according to FactSet.

Hyperscalers in that group are at the center of "the AI storm." But they have appreciated by less than hot chip stocks, making them less vulnerable to a pullback, according to Norton.

The market seems to be "calling the wrestling match after the first takedown instead of waiting to see how it plays out over time," she said. "I don't think we know who the winners and losers are because we don't know exactly how customers and enterprises are going to change their behavior and interact with AI."

While the U.S. equities market's stumble in October was largely triggered by a selloff in the technology sector and Big Tech due to AI anxiety, an equal-weight version of the S&P 500 pulled off a gain as the average stock appeared to do well week after week.

The Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF RSP rallied almost 5% in October, ending Friday with a fourth straight week of gains, according to FactSet data. By contrast, the S&P 500 booked a monthly loss of 0.9%, falling for a third straight week to reduce its 2026 gain to 10.7%, according to Dow Jones Market Data.

-Christine Idzelis

data.title: Next Technology Holding may sell $450M in Bitcoin after Binance hack
data.description:
A Nasdaq-listed company valued at roughly $8 million says it may part with Bitcoin worth about $450 million. That is a stock trading for a sliver of the coins it claims to hold.

Next Technology Holding Inc. (NASDAQ: NXTT) says its board has authorized selling or borrowing against its entire stash of 5,833 BTC. The trigger was the security breach at Binance, which pushed the board to rethink the risks of holding crypto at all.

According to the deep research findings, the board approval took effect on October 30, 2026. It came one day after Binance reported a hot wallet incident on October 29 that compromised approximately $6.3 billion.

A hot wallet is the exchange equivalent of a cash register. It stays connected to the internet for fast withdrawals, which also makes it the most tempting target in the building.

Binance linked the incident to North Korean actors. Approximately $3 billion of the stolen assets have reportedly been frozen through cooperation with issuers and partners.

NXTT's resolution covers two paths. The company can sell the Bitcoin outright, or it can pledge the coins as collateral for loans.

The board handed the CEO authority over timing and method. The stated goals are to reduce market exposure and improve liquidity.

The holdings are valued at approximately $450-480 million, depending on the Bitcoin price used. The company's market capitalization sits at roughly $7-8 million.

NXTT says none of its Bitcoin is held through Binance. So the exchange breach did not directly touch its coins, at least by the company's account.

The board instead pointed to broader worries about exchange security. It also cited quantum computing, a longer-range concern for anyone holding digital assets.

The more pressing issue for investors may be verification. NXTT's filings do not name its institutional custodians, and they provide no wallet addresses that would let outsiders confirm the coins on-chain.

Without that disclosure, shareholders are working on trust. Telling investors your coins are safe while declining to show where they sit is a bit like a magician insisting the rabbit is definitely in the hat.

The company first disclosed Bitcoin purchases in 2023. It then ramped up its holdings significantly through 2024 and 2025, funding the buys through capital raises.

Per the research findings, NXTT acquired its 5,833 BTC at an average cost basis of approximately $30,000 to $31,386 per coin. That puts the total outlay at around $175-183 million.

If those figures hold, the position carries a large paper gain against its current valuation of approximately $450-480 million. Selling would lock in that gain rather than leaving it exposed to price swings.

NXTT has not bought additional Bitcoin since mid-2025. So the stash has been sitting static for some time before this week's decision.

For NXTT shareholders, the central puzzle is the valuation gap. The market is pricing the company at a tiny fraction of the Bitcoin it reports owning.

The lack of custodian names and wallet addresses likely feeds that skepticism. If NXTT sells or borrows against the coins, investors will want to see where the proceeds go.

For the Bitcoin market, a 5,833 BTC sale is meaningful but not enormous. The CEO controls timing and method, so a staggered sale or a loan structure could soften any impact.

The pledge option deserves attention too. Borrowing against Bitcoin keeps the coins on the books but adds leverage, which introduces liquidation risk if prices fall sharply.

data.title: Alphabet’s record plunge, Intel’s 30% collapse: tech’s brutal week of reckoning
data.description:
A broad selloff in technology stocks gathered pace this week, with chipmakers, cloud computing groups, cybersecurity companies and software providers all sharply lower. Several of the sector’s biggest names lost billions of dollars in market value after reporting earnings or issuing forecasts that disappointed investors

The iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF fell 5.52% for the week, while the Dow Jones U.S. Software Index lost more than 3%. The Nasdaq Composite declined 1.95%, as of mid-day Friday.

Star analyst Dan Ives described the week as “absolutely brutal” for technology investors, saying the disruption from AI was becoming increasingly visible in corporate earnings.

Alphabet suffered its biggest one-day percentage decline on record on Thursday, falling as much as 13% and wiping out roughly $500B in market value. Google reported a rare earnings miss on slower growth in search advertising and a sharp increase in AI spending.

Intel shares plunged about 30% on Friday after the chipmaker issued a fourth-quarter forecast well below Wall Street expectations, warning that weakness in the personal computer market could persist through the first half of 2027.

INTC decline also dragged down semiconductor stocks. The PHLX Semiconductor Sector index fell 9%. AMD dropped 11%, Broadcom and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing each fell 6%, and Micron and Nvidia each lost 5%. SanDisk shares fell 12% on Friday despite reporting better-than-expected quarterly results and issuing stronger guidance and an eight-for-one stock split.

Amazon shares shed roughly 7% following its earnings report, as its aggressive investment plans overshadowed growth in its cloud computing business. Microsoft offered a relative bright spot, with shares down about just 2% since its results. Though it moved to raise $25B through a bond offering.

ServiceNow shares tumbled more than 25% on Thursday after the enterprise software company issued a weaker-than-expected forecast for subscription growth, reviving concerns about the potential impact of AI on traditional software businesses.

Fortinet shares plunged about 27%. Although the company beat third-quarter earnings and revenue estimates, investors were disappointed by slower product revenue growth and a reduction in its full-year services revenue outlook.

Selloff spread to other software and cybersecurity companies, with Zscaler falling 7.5%, Okta losing 7.1%, Rubrik declining 5.3%, Palo Alto Networks dropping 5%, Cloudflare shedding 4.9%, CrowdStrike falling 4.6% and SentinelOne losing 3.5%, since Thursday. Twilio shares tumbled 19% on Friday despite the company beating third-quarter earnings and revenue estimates, but analysts called its smaller-than-expected beat.

The tech sell-off represented a moment for long thought rather than a full market reckoning, according to Matt Orton, chief market strategist at Raymond James.

"This pivotal tech earnings week has been a tale of two cities for tech investors…bringing a painful week to the tech bulls although the underlying drivers of the AI Revolution are even more defined going forward in our view," Ives said.

data.title: US President Trump Says Binance Claims To Have Hack 'Pretty Much Under Control,' But Warns Digital Money Has Always Been ‘A Little Bit Dangerous’
data.description:
Key points:
  • President Trump said on Friday his administration was “looking at” the Binance hack.
  • Trump acknowledged that Binance has “it pretty much under control.”
  • He said he has always felt digital money was “a little bit dangerous” because “people never see the money anymore.”

President Donald Trump said that Binance (BNB) told officials it had the fallout from its multibillion-dollar hack “pretty much under control,” while saying that he long felt that digital money was “a little bit dangerous.”

Speaking at the White House on Friday, Trump was asked whether the hack should be tied to a North Korean hacker group. “We’re looking at that,” he said. Trump added that Binance had pledged to make users whole. “They say they’re going to get it back. They’re saying they’re guaranteeing it or something,” he said.

He then pointed to the risks. He compared crypto with traditional payments, such as signing a check. “People never see the money anymore,” he said, adding that he had always felt it was “a little bit dangerous.” Still, he said, “they say they have it pretty much under control.”

Trump also told reporters in the Oval Office that authorities are not sure if North Korea was behind it, but said officials are investigating.

Despite the hack, Binance Coin’s price, the native token of BNB Chain, traded relatively flat over the past 24 hours. On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment around BNB moved to ‘bearish’ from ‘bullish’ zones, while chatter around it stayed at ‘high’ levels over the past day.

What Happened

Binance was hit by a hack on Thursday, with losses reported over $6 billion. Blockchain investigators ZachXBT, Blockaid and TRM Labs had said North Korea was likely behind the attack. The exchange said it had reserved more than $6.34 billion of company funds to cover users’ losses. It is also working to recover about $3 billion in frozen assets.

Why North Korean Hackers Are Different From Others

TRM Lab’s Global Head of Policy Ari Redbord said on the Bankless podcast that North Korean hackers " don't really care if [they] lose some [money] here or there." Redbord added that “They lost a lot last night, but they also made off with, arguably, what would in and of itself be the largest hack ever by 2x, right?”. According to him the hackers “care a lot less about getting caught because no one's going to jail. There's never going to be an extradition, and there's likely not going to be a criminal prosecution of any kind.”

The breach rattled crypto markets, as more than $1.6 billion in leveraged bets were wiped out, and Bitcoin (BTC) fell to a six-week low near $77,300. Following this, the CFTC Chairman Michael Selig said that “the blockchain gives us a very good shot” at tracking the stolen funds.

Not Binance’s First Breach

Binance has been hit by major attacks before, when in October 2022, an attacker exploited a bridge on BNB Chain and minted about 2 million BNB, worth roughly $570 million at the time. Then in May 2019, hackers stole about 7,000 Bitcoin, then worth roughly $40 million, from the exchange’s hot wallet. Binance covered the losses from its emergency fund.

At more than $6 billion, Thursday’s hack is the largest hacks on the chain, followed by ByBit hack, where $1.5 billion worth of Ethereum (ETH) was stolen by North Korea’s Lazarus Group.

data.title: Poland's president accuses Tusk of forced takeover of country's top court
data.description:
Polish President Karol Nawrocki on Saturday accused Prime Minister Donald Tusk of staging a forced takeover of the country's top court after the head of the court, an ally of the previous far right government, was suspended.

Late on Friday, the Constitutional Tribunal said its longest-serving judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska had suspended Bogdan Swieczkowski, the tribunal's president and an appointee of Tusk's hard-right predecessor, and was now in charge of the court.

The move escalated a battle between Nawrocki, an ally of the previous nationalist government, and Prime Minister Donald Tusk's pro-European government over control of the judiciary.

"Tonight, there was a breach of public order in the Republic of Poland and a forcible takeover of a constitutional body," Nawrocki said in a statement read by an aide outside the court early on Saturday, after the president had turned back mid-flight from a trip to Africa to address the situation.

He headed straight to the court where riot police were out in force as several hundred protesters demanded Swieczkowski's reinstatement.

Nawrocki called for urgent political consultations.

Tusk, writing on X, said his government was seeking to restore the rule of law, which the European Union had accused his predecessors — the Law and Justice Party — of subverting.

"This process is difficult, at times even painful, and requires decisive action. There is no other way," he said.

LONG-RUNNING POLITICAL DISPUTE

A long-running political dispute over the Constitutional Tribunal has effectively paralysed the institution, with the pro-European government and the nationalist president refusing to recognise appointees put forward by the other side.

The dispute dates back to 2015, when the Law and Justice sought to appoint judges to seats already filled by the previous government.

Its nominees gained a majority on the Constitutional Tribunal, while critics at home and abroad said the court no longer met the standards of an independent and impartial tribunal established by law.

After Tusk's coalition took office in 2023 it pledged to restore the rule of law and reform the court, but Law and Justice ally Nawrocki has acted to thwart those efforts since his election as president in 2025.

Earlier this year, Nawrocki refused to swear in three of six judges nominated by parliament, while Swieczkowski, a former deputy justice minister in the Law and Justice administration, declined to seat judges elected by the current parliamentary majority.

Last month, parliament appointed Tusk ally Maciej Berek to the tribunal, which critics said undermined the government's stated goal of restoring checks and balances.

data.title: Mukesh Ambani stocks: Reliance Industries vs Jio Platforms shares compared - RIL or JPL? What to buy? Experts' views
data.description:
New Delhi, Oct. 31 -- Mukesh Ambani stocks | Reliance Industries vs Jio Platforms shares: The two Mukesh Ambani-led companies, Reliance Industries Ltd (RIL) and Jio Platforms Ltd (JPL), declared their respective Q2 Results 2026 on Friday. Both companies delivered promising Q2 numbers: RIL reported improved margins in its oil-to-chemicals (O2C) business, while JPL posted strong EBITDA margins, cash reserves, and a rise in ARPU.

According to stock market experts, both Mukesh Ambani-owned stocks are expected to open gap-up on Monday. However, they said that the situation might become tricky for those investors, who want to buy either of these two Mukesh Ambani's stocks.

Decoding Reliance Industries' Q2 Results 2026, Avinash Gorakshkar, Founder of Avinash Mentor Research, said, "Reliance Industries reported strong YoY growth during the July to September 2026 quarter on the consolidated revenue, EBITDA, and net profit front. This could become possible due to the massive recovery in the Oil-to-Chemicals (O2C) EBITDA, which grew about 70% YoY to around Rs.25,200 crore during the September 2026 quarter."

Gorakshkar said that O2C recovery is expected to continue in the next quarter as well, and hence the market is estimating strong Q3 results 2026 from Reliance Industries.

During the July to September 2026 quarter, Reliance's consolidated revenue grew 27.80% YoY to Rs.3,62,268 crore, EBITDA grew 23.9% YoY to Rs.62,409 crore, and the Profit After Tax (PAT) or net profit shot up 33.80% YoY to Rs.29,550 crore.

Speaking on Jio Platforms Q2 Results 2026, Avinash Gorakshkar said, "Like RIL, JPL too posted strong YoY growth in consolidated revenue, EBITDA and net profit. This could become possible on subscriber additions pushing the total user base to 542.4 million (including 300 million 5G users and 30 million fixed-broadband homes), with Average Revenue Per User (ARPU) climbing to Rs.218.8."

data.title: Navi Mumbai Airport: Here is why Emirates and Air France-KLM are resisting shifting international flights from Mumbai
data.description:
New Delhi, Oct. 31 -- Earlier this week, Akasa Air announced that it will shift the Mumbai-Jeddah operations from Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport (CSMIA) to Navi Mumbai International Airport (NMIA), making it the latest airline to move some of its flights to the new airport. Earlier, IndiGo and Air India had also announced that they will move some of their international operations to Navi Mumbai International Airport.

This comes as Mumbai airport operator Mumbai International Airport Ltd (MIAL) wants to transfer some five million passengers annually by March 2027 for Terminal 1B development work. While airlines based in India have complied with the request, several foreign carriers are still reluctant.

This includes Emirates and Air France-KLM, who have cited concerns about NMIA infrastructure.

According to The Indian Express, Emirates has raised questions about NMIA's capacity to support large international airline operations. Air France-KLM has opposed its services between Mumbai and Navi Mumbai, terming the arrangements as "operationally inefficient".

Meanwhile, on Wednesday, representatives of more than 35 airlines and Mumbai airport officials discussed the transition plan for partially shifting international flights, with some carriers seeking more time to decide on the relocation of operations.

MIAL initially planned to implement the partial shifting of international operations from October 25 and later deferred the deadline till March 2027 following concerns raised by various foreign airlines about the transition plan.

Against this backdrop, more than 35 members of the Airline Operators' Committee (AOC) and MIAL officials met for over one-and-a-half hours on Wednesday to discuss the issues related to the shifting of international operations to the Navi Mumbai International Airport (NMIA).

At the meeting, MIAL requested airlines to share their transition plans by November 3 and they were also assured that the temporarily transitioned international traffic of 5 mppa will be fully restored back to Mumbai Airport once the T2 expansion is completed, PTI, citing sources, reported.

Many of the airlines sought time till the next winter schedule that starts in October 2027 for relocation of the international flights, they added.

A source told PTI that airlines have insisted that T1 redevelopment should be done in a phased manner and rejected any unilateral decision by MIAL for reduction of slots from the next summer schedule starting from March 2027.

Mumbai airport has the capacity to handle around 55 million passengers annually, while NMIA is designed to handle 20 million passengers in its initial phase. Both are operated by Adani Airport Holdings Limited (AAHL).

With renovation of Terminal 1 (T1) at the Mumbai airport set to start next year, MIAL wants airlines to partially shift their international flights from Terminal 2 (T2) to NMIA so that the vacated space at T2 will be utilised by the carriers for domestic operations. The renovation of T1 is estimated to be completed by 2030.

Initially, AAHL asked airlines to cut 33 per cent of their international flights or shift them to NMIA by October 25, also the start of the winter schedule.

Following opposition from the operating airlines, it was decided to defer the deadline by a few weeks.

Earlier this month, in a meeting of representatives of AAHL and airlines, it was decided that the partial shifting of international flights to the Navi Mumbai airport would be deferred till the summer schedule that commences in March 2027.

data.title: New Year travel trends: Indians opt for cruises, Lakshadweep and spiritual holidays
data.description:
Indian travellers are increasingly looking beyond traditional New Year’s Eve parties and celebrations, opting for holidays that combine cultural experiences, outdoor adventures, cruises and spiritual journeys, according to a press release issued by Thomas Cook (India) Limited and SOTC Travel.

The travel companies said that year-end holiday preferences are changing, with travellers seeking experiences that go beyond the midnight countdown, including Northern Lights excursions in Europe, cultural celebrations in Japan, premium island holidays and pilgrimage trips within India.

“New Year travel is increasingly about combining the excitement of celebration with the opportunity to discover a destination and its experiences,” said Rajeev Kale, President and Country Head - Holidays, MICE and Visa, Thomas Cook (India) Limited.

He said Indian travellers are looking to make the occasion memorable through different experiences, ranging from watching New Year fireworks over Sydney Harbour to exploring European festive markets and Alpine landscapes.

“Indian travellers are looking to make the occasion memorable through distinctive experiences, whether it is watching the New Year fireworks over Sydney Harbour, exploring Europe’s festive markets and Alpine landscapes, experiencing multiple destinations on a cruise or choosing a premium island escape like Lakshadweep or a spiritual journey in India,” Kale said.

Northern Lights, Japan’s traditions attract travellers

According to the companies’ release, destinations such as Finland, Norway, Sweden and Iceland are among the options for travellers seeking winter experiences, including Northern Lights viewing, husky and reindeer sledding, snowmobile excursions and stays in glass igloos.

Japan is another destination being highlighted for its traditional New Year customs, including Hatsumode, the first shrine or temple visit of the year, while Southeast Asian destinations offer cultural experiences alongside festive celebrations.

Pilgrimage and island holidays gain traction

Closer to home, spiritual tourism is also gaining momentum, with travellers seeking faith-based experiences during the year-end holiday season.

The companies said pilgrimage destinations such as Char Dham, Mahakaleshwar Temple in Ujjain, Tirupati and Vaishno Devi continue to attract travellers looking to combine holidays with prayer and reflection.

Premium island holidays are also emerging as an option for domestic travellers. Thomas Cook India and SOTC Travel have introduced direct charter flights from Bengaluru to Lakshadweep for the year-end season to make the island destination more accessible.

Cruises offer multi-destination experiences

Cruises are another option for travellers seeking to combine New Year celebrations with visits to multiple destinations, with itineraries covering Southeast Asia, the Middle East, the Mediterranean and Australia-New Zealand.

SD Nandakumar, President and Country Head - Holidays and Corporate Tours, SOTC Travel, said travellers are increasingly seeking to make their holidays more meaningful through different activities and experiences.

“While New Year celebrations remain an important draw, travellers are also looking to make the most of their trips through local traditions, seasonal attractions, outdoor adventures, unique stays and cruise journeys,” he said.

The companies said they are offering group tours and customised holiday packages across domestic and international destinations to cater to these varied travel preferences.

data.title: Amazon and Google both have custom chips. Here's what they said about their future.
data.description:
Amid their respective surges in artificial intelligence-related spending, Amazon and Alphabet have seen strong internal demand for their respective custom chip businesses.

Both companies still rely heavily on Nvidia for access to GPUs and will likely continue to do so for the foreseeable future. However, it's clear the ambitions of both companies go beyond just internal use to generate revenue. Alphabet started selling its tensor processing units externally earlier this year, and Amazon is set to do so with its Trainium offerings in late 2027.

And given the insatiable demand for GPUs and CPUs to run AI models, agents, and more, both tech titans see promising futures that could generate billions of dollars in added revenue.

'Strong demand' for TPUs, with more to come?

For Alphabet, its TPU systems have seen “strong demand” already, CEO Sundar Pichai said. The company started offering them externally starting in the middle of this year.

“We are working hard to bring more capacity online to meet this long-term demand,” Pichai said on the company's third-quarter earnings call. “At the same time, we are seeing strong demand for our TPU systems across a wide range of customers, and we expect that to continue as we scale.”

The company has worked with tech giants such as Meta and Apple , AI model labs like Mirendil and Physical Intelligence, and financial firms like Citadel Securities to utilize its TPUs. In total, nearly 100 customers already use TPUs, and the company expects that trend to continue.

“Given continued strong and accelerating demand, we've recently entered into partnerships to deliver TPU systems with both Crux AI and Oracle, with more in the works,” Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian said on the earnings call.

Yorkville Ives analyst Dan Ives said he was pleased regarding the demand for TPU systems that Alphabet is already seeing, citing it as a “second growth engine on the field the other hyperscalers do not have.”

In recent memory, Alphabet has expanded the distribution for TPUs, including deals with Oracle and Crux AI, Kurian explained. And while the company declined to provide specific financial information for TPU sales, CFO Anat Ashkenazi said there will be a “meaningful revenue ramp in 2027.”

Amazon's chips are growing at triple digits

Amazon said in July that its custom chips business (which includes Graviton and Trainium) had reached a $25B revenue run rate. This week, the company delved further into detail and said chip-related revenue grew at a triple-digit percentage pace year-over-year.

Revenue commitments from its Graviton CPUs and Trainium AI accelerators have each risen more than 20 times. By bringing Trainium outside of Amazon Web Services later next year, that could expand its market considerably, Amazon added.

Amazon CEO Andy Jassy explained “most customers are going to use multiple models,” and said its approach is different from Alphabet when it comes to selling chips externally versus what is used in the cloud. (There is still strong demand for older generations of Amazon's Trainium chips that support the economic longevity of the existing infrastructure.)

“I would say that the number of companies who have a significant cloud business and a chip strong enough to sell externally is effectively two,” Jassy said on the company's earnings call, referring to Alphabet. “So there really aren't many customers that have to grapple with the same type of problem at this type of scale. And at this point, everybody is producing their advanced chips with the same provider. There's only so many chips that provider can provide each year. Everybody gets an allocation. And you have to decide with that allocation how much of it you want to sell externally and how much of it you want to use in your cloud. And there's a trade-off. If you sell externally, you're able to realize more revenue in the short term because you get to recognize the revenue as soon as it leaves your inventory. And on the flip side, if you decide to use it inside your cloud in the form of EC2 instances or Bedrock, you actually will end up driving more absolute revenue and free cash flow from those chips because you get to use them over 5 to 6 years and drive revenue for a longer period of time. You have to really think through what you want to do. To date, I would say that we've taken a different approach in how we've used our chips than the other provider who has the same type of balancing act going on.”

“Our ability to create price performance, scalable chips is going to be a very significant strategic advantage for us at scale, both in our own cost structure as well as building a separate business. And selling external chips really is a very different business than your cloud infrastructure business,” Jassy added.

data.title: ServiceNow CFO says AI disruption to enterprise software narrative is false
data.description:
ServiceNow Chief Financial Officer and President Gina Mastantuono understands the importance of guardrails when an enterprise wants to deploy AI solutions.

"Every business and industry needs a harness for AI," she said in an interview with Seeking Alpha. "Enterprise is very different from consumer. One mistake becomes disastrous in minutes. Ninety percent of organizations worldwide have already had an agentic security incident in the past year. Having the security in place is simply not optional."

"We build safeguards into how we innovate," she added. "ServiceNow does that incredibly well. Our AI Control Tower gives customers the confidence and security to use AI without worry."

ServiceNow reported its third-quarter financial results and outlook on Wednesday night. Despite posting solid results, featuring another quarter of 20% plus year-over-year revenue growth, shares cratered 27% by the time the markets closed on Thursday, erasing three months of share gains in one session.

However, most financial firms remain positive on the stock and the trajectory of the company.

"Key positives are centered around the strong AI activity, with nnACV up 65% YoY, which prompted higher 2026 ACV guidance," said Bank of America analyst Tal Liani. "However, the focal points were the 120bp and 40bp shortfall in 4Q in cRPO and subscription growth guidance, partially explained by accounting and timing. We don't fully subscribe to management's explanation on the quarter's weakness, yet remain constructive on the stock, as we see clear evidence of AI growth and view these fluctuations as growing hiccups."

"With the company guiding to a deceleration in cRPO growth into F4Q and an incremental headwind into FY27, we believe the implied low-20% y/y revenue growth rate for F4Q and preliminary estimate for around 19% growth for FY27 (prior to embedding the acceleration in AI adoption into our estimates) still outlines a robust underlying business with room for upside led by performance, despite the concerns investors might express on a slowdown in the cRPO metric, which is largely on account of revenue drivers moving out of scope of cRPO to a modest extent on a temporary basis," said J.P. Morgan analyst Samik Chatterjee.

Despite the noise around the latest earnings and outlook, ServiceNow remains positive on its AI strategy. It remains model-agnostic, allowing customers to use the closed or open model of their choice. It also formed a new partnership with OpenAI . The partnership expansion includes a new ServiceNow plugin for ChatGPT, enabled by Action Fabric. The companies aim to develop security and risk solutions powered by OpenAI cyber models, a Codex integration in AI Workflow Factory, and voice-driven governance and risk assessment for ServiceNow's Super Intelligence Control Tower.

"Enterprises are deploying at scale, and our momentum continues to accelerate and be strong, but at the same time demand for our core workloads remains strong," Mastantuono said. "AI is pulling our core in a strong way. ServiceNow is able to develop and deploy AI without significant infrastructure investments that a lot of companies are having to spend."

data.title: Jatin Kumar Nayak Takes Charge As IREDA Chairman And MD
data.description:
Former REC executive director (Finance) brings over three decades of experience across power, mining, metals and corporate finance to the renewable energy lender

Jatin Kumar Nayak has assumed charge as Chairman and Managing Director of the Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency (IREDA), the state-owned renewable energy financier, said in a statement on Saturday.

Nayak joins IREDA from REC Ltd, where he served as Executive Director (Finance). His appointment had earlier received approval from the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet (ACC).

The appointment brings a finance and power-sector professional with more than three decades of experience to the leadership of IREDA, which finances renewable energy projects in India.

Professional Background And Sector Experience

Before joining IREDA, Nayak served as Executive Director (Finance) at REC Ltd, a Maharatna central public sector enterprise under the Ministry of Power. He had also worked as Chief Financial Officer of the erstwhile REC Transmission Projects Company Ltd, a subsidiary of REC.

Earlier in his career, he held positions at NHPC Ltd, Hindustan Copper Ltd, National Aluminium Company Ltd (NALCO) and Neelachal Ispat Nigam Ltd. His professional experience spans the power sector and resource-intensive industries, including mining and metals.

Expertise In Financing And Lending Operations

Nayak brings experience in domestic and international resource mobilisation, strategic treasury management and corporate finance. His areas of expertise also include taxation, legal affairs, project appraisal and monitoring, lending operations, loan recovery and stressed asset management.

He holds a Master's degree in Commerce from Utkal University, Bhubaneswar. He is a fellow member of the Institute of Cost and Management Accountants of India and a qualified Company Secretary.

Appointment And Tenure

The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy conveyed the appointment through an order dated 29 October 2026, following approval from the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet. Nayak assumed charge at IREDA's registered office in New Delhi on 30 October.

His appointment is effective until his superannuation on 30 September 2029, or until further orders, whichever is earlier. Following his appointment, Dr Bijay Kumar Mohanty, who was holding the additional charge of CMD while serving as Director (Finance), ceased to hold that responsibility.

data.title: India's Rs 10,000 Cr SME Fund Faces A Critical Test: Who Gets The Money?
data.description:
India's smaller manufacturers need patient capital to scale, but fund managers must balance that need against investment returns, governance standards, and exit requirements

For India’s small and medium manufacturers, access to growth capital is not simply a question of how much money the Government puts into a fund. The more difficult question is whether businesses that need equity to expand can meet the investment criteria of the institutions that will deploy it. A profitable manufacturer with limited financial systems, a long customer-acquisition cycle or an uncertain exit route may struggle to attract institutional capital, even when its expansion plans are commercially viable.

That question now faces the Government’s Rs 10,000 crore SME Growth Fund, which the Union Cabinet approved on 6 October 2026. The fund will channel equity into small and medium enterprises through an Alternative Investment Fund (AIF), with a focus on manufacturers. Its impact, however, will depend on how fund managers assess businesses, balance return expectations with the needs of smaller enterprises and decide which companies are ready to receive institutional investment.

The objective is to help viable businesses expand production capacity, adopt advanced technologies, enter international markets and integrate into global value chains. However, industry experts believe the availability of capital alone may not resolve the problem. The investment structure could determine which businesses qualify, particularly when fund managers must balance commercial returns, governance standards and exit opportunities against the Government's wider objective of expanding access to growth capital.

Kush Gupta, Director, SKG Investments & Advisory, believes the proposed allocation is relatively small compared with the financing requirements of the wider micro, small and medium enterprises (MSME) ecosystem. "The fund is too small to close the gap on its own. A May 2025 SIDBI study estimated the MSME credit gap at about Rs 30 lakh crore, so Rs 10,000 crore is roughly 0.33 per cent of it. Most existing support is aimed at micro firms: PMEGP caps manufacturing project cost at Rs 50 lakh, PM Vishwakarma loans go up to Rs 3 lakh, and the Rs 2,000 crore SRI top up is meant for micro enterprises. SRI has backed 682 MSMEs with Rs 15,442 crore against a Rs 50,000 crore target, which is about 31 per cent deployment," said SKG Investments & Advisory Director Kush Gupta.

The comparison highlights the scale of the financing challenge, although the Rs 30 lakh crore figure represents a broader credit gap and is not directly comparable with an equity investment corpus. The two address different financing requirements. According to Sidbi's Annual Report 2024-25, outstanding credit to MSMEs from scheduled commercial banks increased 14.8 per cent year-on-year to Rs 31.3 lakh crore in FY25. The report also estimated the addressable MSME credit gap at approximately Rs 30 lakh crore.

The Economic Survey 2025-26 further highlights the importance of the sector. MSMEs contributed 31.1 per cent of India's gross domestic product (GDP), 35.4 per cent of manufacturing output and 48.58 per cent of exports. The existing Self-Reliant India (SRI) Fund had supported 682 MSMEs through investments worth Rs 15,442 crore as of 30 November 2025. The new initiative therefore enters an ecosystem where equity support already exists, but the Government sees a structural gap in growth-stage financing for small and medium enterprises.

Investment Readiness Could Decide Access

One of the central challenges is that the requirements of institutional investors may not always match the capabilities of smaller businesses. Equity investment requires enterprises to open their financial records to scrutiny, establish transparent ownership structures and maintain governance standards. Many promoter-led manufacturing businesses have established customers and operational experience but may not have the reporting systems or professional management structures that institutional investors expect.

Rajat Srivastava, Co-founder, CEO and CPO, Df-OS, believes the fund must address this gap rather than restrict its investments to businesses that already meet institutional standards. "The fund should therefore combine patient capital with practical support for professionalisation. Integrity and basic compliance must be entry conditions; more sophisticated management systems can develop against agreed milestones. Otherwise, we risk creating a fund that primarily serves businesses already equipped to raise money," said Srivastava.

This distinction could become particularly important for businesses operating outside established financial centres. The Government's factsheet dated 6 October 2026 recorded approximately 9.78 crore registrations across the Udyam and Udyam Assist platforms. Manufacturing accounted for around 1.93 crore registrations, while trading and services accounted for approximately 4.08 crore and 3.77 crore, respectively.

These registration figures cover the wider MSME ecosystem, including micro enterprises, and should not be confused with the pool of eligible small and medium businesses under the new fund. Gupta also cautions that the investment pipeline could favour businesses located in established financial centres. He argues that fund managers may prefer larger transactions because smaller investments involve comparable due-diligence costs but offer lower absolute returns.

Manufacturing Returns Versus Exit Expectations

The structure of an AIF introduces another consideration: the ability to exit investments within the fund's investment horizon. Unlike conventional bank lending, equity investments require investors to realise returns through a future sale, strategic acquisition, public listing or another exit route. This can influence the type of businesses that receive funding.

Ssonit Rajpurohit, Business Partner, Motilal Oswal Financial Services, believes this could create a disadvantage for otherwise profitable manufacturing enterprises. "The key consideration for AIFs is not just the quality of a business, but also the ability to exit the investment within the fund’s finite life, typically 8-10 years.

A profitable auto-component manufacturer in a tier-three city generating 22 per cent ROCE may be fundamentally strong, yet harder to exit than a technology-led or consumer-facing business with a clearer path to scale, strategic acquisition or public listing. This can influence capital allocation, with businesses offering more visible exit opportunities potentially having an advantage over equally sound manufacturing firms," said Rajpurohit.

His example highlights a potential mismatch between the economics of manufacturing and the return expectations of institutional investors. A manufacturer may generate healthy returns on capital employed (ROCE) and have a stable customer base, but its growth trajectory may not offer the same exit opportunities as a technology or consumer-facing business. This does not mean manufacturing enterprises are inherently less attractive. However, the fund's investment mandate, ticket sizes, holding periods and return expectations will influence how managers assess businesses across sectors.

Abhit Kumar, Founder and Chief Executive Officer,  Integra Robotics Founder  said, “There is a genuine equity funding gap, particularly for businesses where expenditure comes well before revenue. In robotics, developing a working solution is only one stage. Taking it into factories requires investment in production, application engineering, customer integration and after-sales support. Customer validation and purchase decisions also take time, which means capital must support the business through that entire cycle."

His assessment highlights why equity can become important for businesses that need to invest well before commercial returns materialise. Developing industrial technology, establishing production capabilities and building customer support networks require capital that may not generate immediate cash flows.

Bank loans can remain suitable for machinery purchases and capacity expansion where demand and repayment cash flows are predictable. Equity, on the other hand, can support projects with longer gestation periods, although promoters must account for ownership dilution and investor return expectations.

Deployment Needs Greater Transparency

The fund's implementation framework will ultimately determine whether its stated objectives translate into wider access to growth capital. The Government has outlined its broad investment priorities, including manufacturing expansion and support for industrial clusters. However, the selection process, investment ticket sizes, fund-manager arrangements and deployment timelines will determine how businesses access the capital.

The experience of existing equity-support programmes also offers a benchmark. The SRI Fund had supported 682 MSMEs with Rs 15,442 crore in investments as of November 2025, against its stated Rs 50,000 crore investment objective. Its experience makes deployment efficiency and the geographical distribution of investments important areas of assessment for the new initiative.

Gupta has called for greater disclosure of the fund's investment criteria, manager details, ticket sizes and geographical allocation. He also argues that a dedicated share for businesses with turnover below Rs 100 crore and enterprises in non-metropolitan industrial clusters could widen access. The Government will also need to ensure that investment readiness does not become a barrier for otherwise viable businesses. A framework that combines basic compliance requirements with professionalisation support and milestone-linked investments could help address this challenge.

The Rs 10,000 crore commitment creates an opportunity to strengthen India's growth-stage financing ecosystem. But the larger test will be whether the fund can identify businesses that have the capacity to become industrial leaders but lack the institutional connections, financial systems or investor visibility to attract capital independently.

For a manufacturing enterprise in a smaller industrial cluster, access to equity could determine whether it can automate production, fulfil larger orders or enter export markets. For an investment manager, however, the same business must also offer a credible return and an eventual exit. Bridging these two requirements will determine whether the SME Growth Fund expands India's pool of competitive manufacturers or primarily finances businesses that institutional investors already consider investment-ready.

data.title: Reliance Consumer's Q2 Revenue Rises 60% To Rs 8,266 Cr
data.description:
Campa's first-half sales exceeded Rs 5,250 crore, while Independence-led daily essentials generated around Rs 7,000 crore

Reliance Consumer Products or RCPL, the FMCG arm of Reliance Industries, reported gross revenue of Rs 8,266 crore in the July-September quarter of FY27, registering a 60 per cent year-on-year increase. Growth was supported by its beverages and daily essentials portfolios, led by Campa and Independence, respectively.

For the first half of FY27, RCPL's gross revenue stood at Rs 16,900 crore, marking an 80 per cent increase over the corresponding period last year. The figure was equivalent to nearly 80 per cent of the company's full-year revenue in FY26, according to Reliance Industries' investor presentation.

“Our consumer products business kept its growth momentum, with the FMCG brand portfolio gaining further ground among Indian consumers,” Mukesh D. Ambani, Chairman and Managing Director, Reliance Industries said.

However, RCPL did not separately disclose quarterly consolidated profit attributable to shareholders, revenue from operations or earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda). This limits an assessment of the profitability of its expanding FMCG operations.

Six Greenfield Projects To Expand Manufacturing Capacity

RCPL has initiated six integrated greenfield food and beverage manufacturing projects across India as it looks to strengthen its production capabilities. During the September quarter, it also commissioned additional high-speed beverage production lines.

The company, however, did not disclose the investment outlay, locations, proposed production capacities or commissioning timelines for the six projects.

Campa Beverages Cross Rs 5,250 Cr In H1 Sales

The beverages business, led by Campa, recorded first-half sales of more than Rs 5,250 crore, representing approximately 2.1 times its sales in the year-ago period. The performance also took the portfolio beyond 90 per cent of its full-year FY26 sales within the first six months of FY27.

RCPL said it had become India's third-largest non-alcoholic ready-to-drink (NARTD) beverages player, with double-digit market share across several states.

The daily essentials portfolio, led by Independence, generated approximately Rs 7,000 crore in H1 FY27, around 1.7 times the year-earlier level. Edible oils and dry fruits contributed to the segment's growth, while the Independence and Udhaiyam brands supported its pulses business.

The company is also building its presence in home and personal care through brands such as Glimmer. “Home and personal care led by Glimmer is gaining early consumer traction in the market,” Reliance said in its investor presentation.

RCPL attributed the performance across its categories to product-range expansion and wider national distribution. In packaged foods, biscuits remain a focus area, with the company targeting both mass-market and premium consumer segments through its offerings.

The company has also entered the dairy category with ice creams, positioning the products in the accessible premium segment. Made using real dairy cream, the range is available in cone, stick, tub, cup and brick formats.

Campa Expands Overseas Presence

RCPL is also extending its international distribution network, with Campa entering major Australian supermarket chains Coles and Woolworths, supported by local production arrangements.

The company has launched operations in Kenya, adding to its existing presence in Ghana and Nigeria. Its international footprint also includes the UAE, Oman and Malaysia.

Despite the strong year-on-year revenue growth, RCPL's first-half figures indicate a sequential moderation in the September quarter. Based on the reported H1 gross revenue of Rs 16,900 crore and September-quarter revenue of Rs 8,266 crore, the implied June-quarter revenue stood at approximately Rs 8,634 crore. This suggests a sequential decline of around 4.3 per cent. Reliance's investor presentation did not provide an explanation for the movement.

The expansion of manufacturing infrastructure, product categories and overseas distribution reflects Reliance's efforts to scale its consumer products business. However, the absence of separately disclosed profitability figures makes it difficult to assess the earnings contribution and returns from the expansion.

data.title: Reliance Retail Q2 Revenue Rises 6.4%, Ajio Catalogue Expands 23%
data.description:
Reliance Retail's customer transactions grew 7 per cent in Q2, while Ajio expanded its catalogue by 23 per cent and the company's premium and luxury portfolio crossed 1,000 exclusive brand stores

Reliance Retail Ventures or RRVL, the retail arm of Reliance Industries, reported a 6.4 per cent year-on-year increase in gross revenue to Rs 91,716 crore in the July-September quarter, adjusted for the demerger of its Consumer Brands business.

The company’s operating performance was affected by the shift in the festive calendar, with major festivals falling in the December quarter this year. Ebitda, before a one-time impairment charge, stood at Rs 6,228 crore, with a margin of 7.8 per cent.

Reliance Retail attributed the 120-basis-point moderation in its Ebitda margin to the change in festive-season timing, higher input costs and continued investments in expanding its business-to-business (B2B) and digital commerce operations.

On a reported basis, the retail business posted revenue of Rs 91,717 crore, compared with Rs 90,409 crore in the June quarter and Rs 90,544 crore in the corresponding period last year. Ebitda declined to Rs 6,120 crore from Rs 6,309 crore sequentially and Rs 6,817 crore a year earlier. The reported Ebitda margin stood at 6.7 per cent, against 7 per cent in the previous quarter and 7.5 per cent in the year-ago period.

"The new model with fast growing Digital Commerce and B2B channels is working and funded by the profits of offline business," said Isha Ambani, Executive Director of Reliance Retail Ventures.

Reliance Retail Adds 303

Reliance Retail opened 303 stores during the September quarter, taking its total store network to 19,947, a 0.6 per cent increase year-on-year. Its operational retail area stood at 77.5 million square feet.

Customer transactions increased 7 per cent year-on-year, despite the postponement of major festive-season demand to the December quarter, indicating continued consumer engagement, the company said.

JioMart Revenue Climbs 42%

In the grocery business, like-for-like (LFL) growth stood at 3 per cent year-on-year. Reliance Retail focused on regional customer engagement through festive-themed in-store initiatives and introduced its Smart 2.0 format, which incorporates artificial intelligence-enabled ordering. Revenue from its B2B business increased 10 per cent during the quarter.

Its digital grocery platform JioMart recorded 42 per cent revenue growth year-on-year, supported by higher average order values and a 24 per cent increase in units per order. The platform expanded its network to more than 5,000 stores across over 1,000 cities.

Digital commerce accounted for a larger share of the company's business-to-consumer grocery revenue, increasing by 270 basis points year-on-year.

The consumer electronics segment recorded 8 per cent LFL growth, driven by demand for mobiles, laptops, IT peripherals and appliances, alongside brand partnerships. Reliance Retail's after-sales service business, ResQ, completed 97 per cent of service requests within 48 hours.

In fashion and lifestyle, LFL growth stood at 3 per cent year-on-year. Ajio expanded its catalogue by 23 per cent to 3.3 million options, while the company's premium and luxury portfolio crossed 1,000 exclusive brand stores.

During the quarter, Reliance Retail launched Fabletics in India and entered an exclusive partnership with SKIMS.

data.title: OpenAI slashes funding goal by $10B amid tech selloff: FT
data.description:
OpenAI has cut the target for its newest funding round by $10B at a time when the U.S. tech stocks are in a selloff driven by concerns over AI infrastructure buildout, The Financial Times reported, citing people with knowledge of the matter.

The ChatGPT maker is now looking for about $20B in funds at a valuation of roughly $1.25T, down from $1.4T it targeted last month, according to the report. While the company set a Friday deadline for investors to commit, the “first close” is expected to generate ⁠less than $20B after some investors cut their allocations, it ​added.

OpenAI didn’t immediately respond to a request for comments. Last week, citing people familiar with the deal, CNBC reported that the San Francisco-based AI firm is closing in on a funding round that could raise up to $30B.

The company that is seeking a U.S. listing next year was racing to close the funding round partly to get ahead of rival Anthropic’s much-anticipated public debut in mid-November, Reuters had reported previously.

Its revised funding target reflects investor worries over the pace of AI buildout. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell 2% this week, its third straight weekly drop, as quarterly results from Intel and Amazon showed the pace of their massive cash burn amid heavy investments in AI-related development.

data.title: A Top Brazilian Fund Manager Says Despite the Selloff the Country Could Still Be 'Best Positioned for the 21st Century' — Barrons.com
data.description:
By Sabrina Escobar

The surprising outcome of Brazil's presidential elections has put the country's equities through the wringer.

The Ibovespa, Brazil's benchmark index, plummeted 14% on Monday, marking its largest percent decrease since March 2020, while the iShares MSCI Brazil ETF (EWZ) dropped 20%. The move erased most of the indexes' year to date gains, including the surge that followed Brazil's first-round election results earlier this month, which suggested Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro had the advantage over incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

Brazil's financial sector was especially hard hit. Shares of XP, an investment management company and one of Brazil's largest brokerages, had its worst day on record Monday, plummeting near 50%.

Barron's spoke with Artur Wichmann, XP's chief investment officer, about how investors should interpret the election results, and his outlook for Latin America's biggest economy.

This conversation has been edited. Some parts of the interview were previously published in the Barron's Global Signals newsletter.

Barron's: How are you thinking about how the market reacted in the wake of the Brazilian election results?

Artur Wichmann: Brazil is perceived to have one very large macroeconomic Achilles' heel, which is the fiscal situation. We have a combination of three characteristics that together are very toxic: A very elevated debt-to-GDP [ratio] for an emerging market country, a very large fiscal deficit, and a budget that is very rigid [and] constitutionally fixed, which means that it's very difficult to make fiscal policy in Brazil.

If you put those three things together, we have a debt-to-GDP ratio which is on an explosive trajectory. That was what mattered for the markets in this election. We need a president that addresses the fiscal situation. The market knows President Lula, knows he has made some attempts, but Brazil is still in a bad fiscal situation under his mandate. So the market says, this other guy [Bolsonaro] is talking about it. There wasn't a very clear plan, but there were talks of balancing the budgets. So the market votes for fiscal stability.

There are gigantic risk premiums associated with Brazilian assets because of our fiscal vulnerability. So the market says, if there is a possibility of a change in direction for the better in fiscal policy, I'm going to compress risk premiums. And that's exactly what happened the Monday after the first round of presidential elections.

Then Lula won the second round, which was a huge surprise to the market. The market says, we know the fiscal policy under President Lula and we don't like it. So we have to reassign risk premiums to the Brazilian assets, which had been removed because of the assumption that there was going to be a change in the fiscal policy.

Do you think that the market is fairly priced where it is now? When you think about equities, is it still a market that foreign investors should be considering despite the fiscal problem and despite the election result?

Absolutely, if there's one thing you cannot bring through the investment process is any sort of prejudice. You have to judge every asset or every investment opportunity with the basis in its fundamentals.

The opportunities in Brazil are here, but we have to have a consistent fiscal policy. [Lula's] attitude toward fiscal policy has been ambiguous. He hasn't dismissed fiscal concerns as not being relevant. But sometimes he says some things that make the market a little less confident. I think President Lula is a very pragmatic man. He's intelligent. No president wants to face a fiscal crisis right from the get-go. So I think we will have a fiscal policy that is consistent — to a certain extent. But my certainty as far as that isn't great, because there is discord in congress, even within the government's party. You have people that say we have to take care of the fiscal, and others that say it's all orthodox economics, or us bowing to the financial markets.

The political system could take a clue from what the voters said and get a compromise to make fiscal policy that is sustainable. That guarantees the risk premiums converge over time to levels more normal, and then Brazil can become a star. I'm not making that projection, yet.

What I want to convey is that the realm of probabilities in Brazil is very wide. Brazil could be one of the countries that is best positioned for the 21st century. We have cheap renewable energy, which could feed data centers. We have rare earths which could feed semiconductors. We have food, we have arable land. It's the equivalent of a car that's got an extremely good engine and good suspension. But if you don't put in the right tires, then it's all for nothing. So this is a very powerful position — if you use the correct macroeconomic frame.

How does ongoing ambiguity about the path of Lula's fiscal plans factor into the central bank's decision to keep lowering rates?

If the government does the right thing, the central bank could continue to lower interest rates. Interest rates in Brazil, real interest rates in Brazil are extremely high. They are among the highest in the world. And a lot of that is risk premium because people are afraid of [the] unanchoring of inflation expectations, and people are afraid of the currency depreciating a lot.

So for investors, is it about seeing who is well positioned despite the macro challenges?

Yes and no. Brazil's got two big problems, one macro and one micro. The micro is: Brazil is one of the most difficult business environments in the world. To set up a simple bakery in Brazil is an extremely complex process. There was a time that there was a new tax arrangement in Brazil a day. Every single day, the IRS, the environmental agents that were changing the taxation on a daily basis. Imagine how difficult it is just to be on top of that.

So the microeconomic agenda makes that potential that I just told you very difficult to realize. But it's possible. You can look at it, glass half empty, glass half full. If we fix it, Brazil could fly, as did South Korea. But we haven't addressed it in decades, right? Are we going to do it now? I'll tell you in a couple of months.
